tip: Both imperfect: 'vivíamos' + 'teníamos'. Describes a habitual past situation, not a single event.
English says "has felt lonely since..." – Spanish uses plain present: 'se siente sola desde que.' If it's still true now, present tense, no perfect needed.
The 'cuanta más... más' pattern works like English 'the more... the more'.
'Hay que' = literally "there is that..." – Spanish's no-subject must. 'hay que dejar la masa reposar': nobody in particular, everyone in general, has to.
Commands glue pronouns onto the end: 'dámelo' = 'da' + 'me' + 'lo' fused, with an accent added to keep the stress. Compare 'te lo pido' – normal pre-verb order returns.
'Me llamo' = I call myself. The reflexive 'me' refers back to the subject (yo). This is how Spanish usually states names.
'Por' = because of: 'Llegué tarde por el tráfico.' Expresses the cause behind something.
Weather uses 'hacer': 'hace mucho viento' = "it makes much wind." 'viento' is a noun, so it takes 'mucho'; 'muy viento' would be "very wind."
'Por' = in exchange for: 'Lo compré por diez euros.' It marks what you give to get something.
'Gustar' for a person can sound romantic. For plain liking, Spanish flips it: 'me cae bien' – your friend 'falls well' on me. Safe, attraction-free.
'Por' = about or concerning: 'Preguntó por ti.' Use 'por' when asking or worrying about someone.
'Ojalá' descends from Arabic 'law sha Allah' (if God willed) – it expresses a wish, not a fact, so it always takes the subjunctive: 'ojalá haga buen tiempo.'
'Cuando' + a future action uses the subjunctive: 'cuando llegues' (not 'cuando llegas').
Spanish splits waking in two: 'despertar' is waking someone else up. To wake up on your own, you turn the verb back on yourself – 'me despierto', 'I wake myself.'
Subjunctive because the hotel is hypothetical or unknown: 'que tenga'. If the hotel were known, you'd use the indicative.
Don't reach for 'realizar' – that means to carry out a plan. To notice or realize is 'darse cuenta', literally 'give yourself account': here, 'se dé cuenta'.
'Querer que' + subjunctive: wanting someone else to act. Card: 'quiere que la llame' (wants me to call her). Different subjects, so subjunctive.
Clock times run plural: 'a las siete', roughly 'at the sevens', with one exception: 1:00 is 'a la una', singular, because there's only one of it.
'Caerse' = to fall down (accidentally). The reflexive adds an accidental nuance: 'me caí' = I fell (it happened to me).
Same brother, two verbs: 'es alto' – height is who he is; 'está enfermo' – sickness is just today's condition. 'Ser' for identity, 'estar' for state.
'Quedar' for how clothes fit: 'me queda grande' = it's too big on me. Like 'gustar', it uses an indirect object ('me', 'te').
Subjunctive when you describe something unknown or maybe nonexistent: 'que tenga piscina', because this hotel isn't found yet.
'Quedarse dormido' = to fall asleep (accidentally); card: 'me quedo dormido'. 'Quedarse' + adjective means to end up or become: 'quedarse solo', 'quedarse callado'.
'Sepa', not 'sabe': this 'alguien' may not even exist – you're describing a wish, not a found person. Once found, back to indicative: 'conozco a alguien que sabe'.
Two pasts, one scene: 'caminábamos' (imperfect) is the ongoing background action; 'encontramos' (preterite) is the completed event that happened during it.
'Por mucho que' + subjunctive – no matter how much: here 'lo intente', not 'lo intento'.
'Es mejor que' bends the next verb into subjunctive – 'reserves', not 'reservas' – because booking early is a recommendation, not a report of what did happen.
'Coser y cantar' is literally 'to sew and sing' – work so effortless you can carry a tune while doing it. Like English 'piece of cake': measure ease by a mindless pleasure.
Spanish asks how you call yourself: 'te llamas' is the reflexive 'llamarse'. '¿Cómo te llamas?' is literally 'How do you call yourself?' – no word for 'name' in sight.
In 'haciéndolo', the pronoun 'lo' attaches to the end of the '-ndo' form ('haciendo' = doing).
